title: Compilation Error: expected `Result<Value<'_>, Error>`, found `Value<'_>`
body:
When compiling with the following dependencies:

```toml
rquickjs = { version = "0.11", git = "https://github.com/DelSkayn/rquickjs", features = ["loader"], default-features = false }
llrt_modules = { git = "https://github.com/awslabs/llrt", features = [] }
```

I encountered the following compilation error:

```text
Error:    --> /Users/runner/.cargo/git/checkouts/llrt-0a7fdb298878dfd0/22cc670/modules/llrt_buffer/src/buffer.rs:738:13
    |
722 |       let value = match kind {
    |  _________________-
723 | |         NumberKind::BigInt => {
724 | |             let value = match endian {
725 | |                 Endian::Big => i64::from_be_bytes(bytes.try_into().unwrap()),
...   |
728 | |             Value::new_big_int(ctx.clone(), value)
    | |             -------------------------------------- this is found to be of type `Result<rquickjs::Value<'_>, rquickjs::Error>`
...   |
738 | |             Value::new_float(ctx.clone(), value as f64)
    | |             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ expected `Result<Value<'_>, Error>`, found `Value<'_>`
...   |
788 | |         },
789 | |     };
    | |_____- `match` arms have incompatible types
    |
    = note: expected enum `Result<rquickjs::Value<'_>, rquickjs::Error>`
             found struct `rquickjs::Value<'_>`
help: try wrapping the expression in `Ok`
    |
738 |             Ok(Value::new_float(ctx.clone(), value as f64))
    |             +++                                           +
```

GitHub Actions log:

[https://github.com/ahaoboy/rquickjs-llrt-demo/actions/runs/26454577041/job/77884727453](https://github.com/ahaoboy/rquickjs-llrt-demo/actions/runs/26454577041/job/77884727453)

It seems that `Value::new_big_int` now returns `Result<Value, Error>` in `rquickjs 0.11`, while other branches still return `Value`, causing incompatible `match` arm types.

https://github.com/DelSkayn/rquickjs/issues/585

title: Bug in S3 Checksums with CRC64 NVME
body:
We were moving some Lambdas from Node to LLRT this started happening when calling `S3.getObject()`:

```
Error: Checksum mismatch: expected "AAAAAAAAAAA=" but received "yniAaTFQA1g=" 
       in response header "x-amz-checksum-crc64nvme"
```

`yniAaTFQA1g=` is the checksum value we can see in the AWS S3 console for that file.

Configuration attempts with `responseChecksumValidation: "WHEN_REQUIRED"` do not resolve the issue.

---

SDK Version: `@aws-sdk/client-s3 ^3.1031.0`
LLRT Version: `0.8.1`

title: The same module imported with different path does not share the same instance
body:
# Problem

When running with `llrt`, the store is initialized twice and imports within submodules do not share the same instance of the store, leading to `undefined` when using functions from a nested module. This diverges from expected ECMAScript module semantics.

This issue could point to a problem with module caching and singletons for ESM, where separate module loads result in duplicate state.

Environment
- LLRT v0.8.1-beta (darwin, arm64)


## Expected
```bash
$ llrt index.js
store initialized
get bar
get_in_bar bar
```

## Actual
```bash
$ llrt index.js 
store initialized
store initialized
get bar
get_in_bar undefined
```

## Example

**Directory Structure:**
```
.
├── index.js
└── lib
    ├── bar
    │   └── index.js
    └── shared
        └── store.js
```

**index.js**
```js
import { get, set } from './lib/shared/store.js';
import { get_in_bar } from './lib/bar/index.js';

set('foo', 'bar');
console.log('get', get('foo')); // Output: 'bar'
console.log('get_in_bar', get_in_bar('foo')); // Output: 'bar'
```

**lib/shared/store.js**
```js
const store = {};

console.log('store initialized');

export function set(key, value) {
  store[key] = value;
}

export function get(key) {
  return store[key];
}
```

**lib/bar/index.js**
```js
import { get } from '../shared/store.js';

export function get_in_bar(key) {
  return get(key);
}
```
author: dishuostec

comments.author: nabetti1720
comments.body:
Thank you for the report. We were able to reproduce the issue here as well.

As you pointed out, we are currently loading from a file every time, so we need to incorporate a mechanism like a module cache. I will look into it. :)

title: parsing json via import() fails for escaped characters
body:
### Description
Parsing JSON via `await import()` fails for escaped characters like `\"`.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Create a file test.json with this content: `["\"Test"]`
2. Run llrt in the same directory as the test json file e.g. `.\llrt.exe`
3. Run `await import("./test.json")`

### Expected Behavior
The JSON is parsed correctly as
`{ default: [ '"Test' ] }`

### Current Behavior
Parsing fails with error:
`Error: "[""Test"]
" not valid JSON at index 0`

### Context
Nodejs parses the same json test file correctly using the with type json attribute.
`node`
`await import("./test.json",{with: {type: "json"}})`
`{ default: [ '"Test' ] }
`
author: Steelhasher

comments.author: Steelhasher
comments.body: Thank you for fixing this quickly. I really appreciate your work on LLRT! I’ve been using it for a while now in my services.

title: fix: hostname matching allows subdomain bypass via ends_with
body:
## Description

The url_match() function uses `host.ends_with(entry.host())` to match hostnames.
This allows an attacker to bypass the allowlist: if "example.com" is allowed,
then "notexample.com", "evilexample.com", or "notexample.com.evil.com" would ALL match
because "notexample.com".ends_with("example.com") is true. This is a critical
security flaw in a runtime designed for Lambda/serverless workloads.


**Severity**: `high`
**File**: `modules/llrt_fetch/src/security.rs`

## Expected Behavior

The code should handle this case properly to avoid unexpected errors or degraded quality.

title: Determining the AWS SDK version at runtime?
author: perpil

comments.author: nabetti1720
comments.body:
```
import packageJson from '@aws-sts/client/package.json' with { type: 'json' };
```

The package.json file is not bundled, so it cannot be obtained in this way. Even if you manage to obtain it, I think it will be a local copy, not a bundled one.

For example, in Node.js, you can use `globalThis.process.versions` to refer to the versions of dependent components. It might be useful if LLRT could also embed version information during the build process.

```
% node -e "console.log(globalThis.process.versions);"
{
  node: '24.10.0',
  acorn: '8.15.0',
  ada: '3.3.0',
  amaro: '1.1.4',
  ares: '1.34.5',
  brotli: '1.1.0',
  cjs_module_lexer: '2.1.0',
  cldr: '47.0',
  icu: '77.1',
  llhttp: '9.3.0',
  modules: '137',
  napi: '10',
  nbytes: '0.1.1',
  ncrypto: '0.0.1',
  nghttp2: '1.67.1',
  openssl: '3.6.0',
  simdjson: '4.0.7',
  simdutf: '6.4.0',
  sqlite: '3.50.4',
  tz: '2025a',
  undici: '7.16.0',
  unicode: '16.0',
  uv: '1.51.0',
  uvwasi: '0.0.23',
  v8: '13.6.233.10-node.28',
  zlib: '1.2.12',
  zstd: '1.5.7'
}
```

comments.author: nabetti1720
comments.body:
In that case, we need to consider whether to manage it as a single version under `@aws-sdk` or separately for each component.

Personally, I think that currently, dependency updates are handled in a way that keeps the versions of each component constant, so managing them with a single version should be sufficient.

comments.author: perpil
comments.body: I'm ok with a single version under `@aws-sdk` too.

## llrt:timezone

Lightweight timezone support for LLRT. Provides timezone offset calculations and a minimal `Intl.DateTimeFormat` implementation for dayjs and similar library compatibility.

```typescript
interface Timezone {
  /**
   * Get the UTC offset in minutes for a timezone at a given time.
   * Returns a positive value for timezones ahead of UTC (e.g., 540 for Asia/Tokyo)
   * and a negative value for timezones behind UTC (e.g., -420 for America/Denver).
   * Automatically handles DST transitions.
   */
  getOffset(timezone: string, epochMs: number): number;

  /**
   * List all available IANA timezone names.
   */
  list(): string[];
}

declare var Timezone: Timezone;

export { Timezone };
```

### Example

```javascript
import { Timezone } from "llrt:timezone";

// Get current offset for Denver (handles DST automatically)
const offset = Timezone.getOffset("America/Denver", Date.now());
// Returns -420 (UTC-7) in winter, -360 (UTC-6) in summer

// Check DST transition
const beforeDst = new Date("2024-03-09T12:00:00Z").getTime();
const afterDst = new Date("2024-03-11T12:00:00Z").getTime();
console.log(Timezone.getOffset("America/Denver", beforeDst)); // -420
console.log(Timezone.getOffset("America/Denver", afterDst)); // -360

// List all available timezones
const zones = Timezone.list();
```

### Intl.DateTimeFormat

LLRT provides a minimal `Intl.DateTimeFormat` implementation focused on timezone support. This enables libraries like dayjs to work with timezone conversions transparently.

```javascript
// Create a formatter for a specific timezone
const formatter = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", {
  timeZone: "America/Denver",
  hour12: false,
  year: "numeric",
  month: "2-digit",
  day: "2-digit",
  hour: "2-digit",
  minute: "2-digit",
  second: "2-digit",
});

// Format a date
const date = new Date("2022-03-02T15:45:34Z");
console.log(formatter.format(date)); // "03/02/2022, 08:45:34"

// Get formatted parts
const parts = formatter.formatToParts(date);
// [{ type: "month", value: "03" }, { type: "literal", value: "/" }, ...]

// Get resolved options
const options = formatter.resolvedOptions();
console.log(options.timeZone); // "America/Denver"
```

### Date.prototype.toLocaleString with timezone

`Date.prototype.toLocaleString` is enhanced to support the `timeZone` option:

```javascript
const date = new Date("2022-03-02T15:45:34Z");

// Convert to Denver time
console.log(date.toLocaleString("en-US", { timeZone: "America/Denver" }));
// "03/02/2022, 8:45:34 AM"

// Convert to Tokyo time
console.log(date.toLocaleString("en-US", { timeZone: "Asia/Tokyo" }));
// "03/03/2022, 12:45:34 AM"
```

### Using with dayjs

The timezone module enables dayjs timezone support without polyfills:

```javascript
const dayjs = require("dayjs");
const utc = require("dayjs/plugin/utc");
const timezone = require("dayjs/plugin/timezone");

dayjs.extend(utc);
dayjs.extend(timezone);

// Convert between timezones
const date = dayjs("2022-03-02T15:45:34Z");
console.log(date.tz("America/Denver").format()); // "2022-03-02T08:45:34-07:00"
console.log(date.tz("Asia/Tokyo").format()); // "2022-03-03T00:45:34+09:00"

// Get start of day in a specific timezone
const denver = date.tz("America/Denver");
console.log(denver.startOf("day").format()); // "2022-03-02T00:00:00-07:00"
```

title: Bug: createRequire broken in 0.8.0-beta+
body:
Sorry I didn't notice this earlier.

Previously with 0.7.0-beta the following code was working, but with 0.8.0-beta+ it throws the error "TypeError: not a function"

```js
import { createRequire } from "node:module";

var __require = createRequire(import.meta.url);
console.log(__require('node:fs'));
console.log(__require('node:events'));
```

### Reproduction

1. Create file test.js with above content
2. Run `llrt test.js`

### Workaround

Replace `createRequire(import.meta.url)` with `require`.

(Minor side note, unrelated to this issue, the release 0.8.1-beta still prints 0.8.0-beta if called with `--version`.)

title: Transition from `chrono/chrono-tz` to `jiff`
body:
I found a crate that may be a good replacement for chrono/chrono-tz.

jiff - A datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success.
https://github.com/BurntSushi/jiff

> Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success. The focus of this library is providing high level datetime primitives that are difficult to misuse and have reasonable performance. Jiff supports automatic and seamless integration with the Time Zone Database, DST aware arithmetic and rounding, formatting and parsing zone aware datetimes losslessly, opt-in Serde support and a whole lot more.

One of its features is that if the target OS has a TimezoneDatabase, it will be used, leading to a smaller footprint.

There are still some rough edges, but we've managed to reduce the binary size by about 900kb.

```
before: use chrono and chrono-tz
% du -k target/aarch64-apple-darwin/release/llrt
12816   target/aarch64-apple-darwin/release/llrt

after: use jiff
% du -k target/aarch64-apple-darwin/release/llrt
11916   target/aarch64-apple-darwin/release/llrt

title: Is it possible to remove `ring` from the native implementation of SubtleCrypto?
body:
The `llrt_crypto` backend is now selectable, but it looks like the native backend still has a `ring` dependency.

use ring::{

title: Strange behavior of buffer.subarray
body:
It seems that calling `subarray` again on the result of `subarray` will return the corresponding part of the original buffer.

How to reproduce:
```js
// check.js
import { Buffer } from 'buffer';

const origin = Buffer.from('Hello, World!');
const sub = origin.subarray(7, 12);

console.log('origin.toString():', origin.toString());
console.log('sub.toString():', sub.toString());

console.log('origin.subarray(1, 3).toString():', origin.subarray(1, 3).toString());
console.log('sub.subarray(1, 3).toString():', sub.subarray(1, 3).toString());
```

Run with LLRT v0.7.0-beta (darwin, arm64):
```shell
$ llrt check.js 
origin.toString(): Hello, World!
sub.toString(): World
origin.subarray(1, 3).toString(): el
sub.subarray(1, 3).toString(): el
```

Run with node v22.21.0
```shell
$ node check.js 
origin.toString(): Hello, World!
sub.toString(): World
origin.subarray(1, 3).toString(): el
sub.subarray(1, 3).toString(): or
```

title: Support for `AsyncLocalStorage` from `async_hooks`
body:
Although LLRT implements the `async_hooks` module, it does not expose `AsyncLocalStorage`.
https://nodejs.org/api/async_context.html#class-asynclocalstorage

It seems that several well-known packages have adopted or are considering adopting it, so if it is implemented in LLRT, I think it will be able to accommodate new use cases.

Some packages that already use it include:
- hono/context-storage: https://github.com/honojs/hono/blob/main/src/middleware/context-storage/index.ts
- @opentelemetry/context-async-hooks : https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-js/blob/main/packages/opentelemetry-context-async-hooks/src/AsyncLocalStorageContextManager.ts

Information on the packages we plan to adopt is as follows:
https://github.com/aws-powertools/powertools-lambda-typescript/issues/2050#issuecomment-3341946805
> Additionally, I'd encourage LLRT to add support for `AsyncLocalStorage` from `async_hooks`; even for Logger & Metrics (core utilities) we'll most likely start using this API in the next couple months to allow for future use cases.
> 
> There's even a new package called `@aws/lambda-invoke-store` ([repo](https://github.com/awslabs/aws-lambda-invoke-store)) that, quoting its readme "is designed to be integrated with the AWS Lambda Node.js Runtime Interface Client (RIC)", which means applications targeting versions of Node.js managed runtimes that use this package, might rely on `AsyncLocalStorage` and not work on LLRT.

Additionally, `InvokeStore` imported via `@aws/lambda-invoke-store` should be exposed as `globalThis.awslambda.InvokeStore`.

title: Rerun the benchmark?
body:
Is it possible to rerun the [benchmark](https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/blob/main/example/functions/src/v3-lib.mjs) with the latest release? Since January 2024, the llrt binaries have grown 2+ MB. I've been doing some coldstart benchmarking to compare LLRT standard sdk with Node 22.  My test using arm in us-east-2 instantiates a STS client and invokes get-caller-identity. It isn't quite the same as a ddb put, but it's similar enough that I'd expect the http and λ times to be close to yours on coldstarts. In the table below http means time recorded from the client and λ is time from the invocation logs like yours. Overhead means http - λ. I'm noticing that the overhead in the cold start is higher for LLRT than when using the Node 22 runtime by about 50 ms. I also notice that my p50 for http is ~40 ms higher than your benchmark, but λ is ~17 ms higher. I suspect the increase in binary size is the main contributor, but if you can rerun the benchmarks that will help narrow down what is causing the deltas.



| Test | memory | samples | p0(http) | p50(http) | p99(http) | p50(overhead) | p0(λ) | p50(λ) | p99(λ) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LLRT v.0.7.0-beta| 128 | 140 | 186 | 275 | 357 | 193 | 61 | 81 | 128 |

author: perpil

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body:
Hi @perpil. Sure thing, we should rerun the benchmark. And you are also right that the overall increased cold start time is due to binary size due to disk read performance (and decompression) on Lambda.

I also think you should benchmark with similar memory size. In your current test, Node has 4x more memory which also means 4x more CPU (and CPU time) which makes it very biased.

Also get-caller-identity for STS is quite slow which also means that a lot of duration (for both Node and LLRT is spent waiting) that affects the test. For example say there is 100ms latency for the call and LLRT finnishes in 125 and node 200. On paper this makes LLRT 60% faster (200/100), but it's actually 4x faster (100/25).

Without a closer look at the benchmark bundle files on Node I also suspect that the overheard comes from shipping pure JS Code for Node vs with LLRT shipping the executable + JS Code.

That being said, a lot of the recent size increases in LLRT comes from the WebCrypto APIs that are in pure Rust. We're working on building variants of LLRT that uses static and runtime loaded OpenSSL instead. This is significantly shrink the binary size and only introduce a cold start penalty if you actually use WebCrypto APIs which most use cases don't. Additionally that increased cold start time is offset by increased performance of OpenSSL and libcrypto vs pure rust crypto implementations. The downside of this approach is that it requires OpenSSL/libcrypto to exists (which it does in Lambda). That's why different versions of LLRT will use different Crypto Providers, where the Lambda version will dynamically load OpenSSL symbols at runtime on demand when this feature is completed.

title: Response.json inconsistencies with Node
body:
In debugging [an issue with the new PowerTools Event Handler library](https://github.com/aws-powertools/powertools-lambda-typescript/issues/4499), an inconsistency between Node and LLRT came up with `Response.json`.

The full details are in the linked issue but when running the following code:

```javascript
const stuff = Response.json({ message: 'pong' });
console.log('stuff', { stuff }); // 
console.log('stuff body', await stuff.text()); // [object Object]
```

node logs:

```
[/aws/lambda/PongFn] 11:44:28 PM 2025-09-16T21:44:28.464Z       3d8cb49f-ec3f-4333-b08f-a1d00fe4acd1    INFO    stuff {
  stuff: Response {
    status: 200,
    statusText: '',
    headers: Headers { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
    body: ReadableStream { locked: false, state: 'readable', supportsBYOB: true },
    bodyUsed: false,
    ok: true,
    redirected: false,
    type: 'default',
    url: ''
  }
}
[/aws/lambda/PongFn] 11:44:28 PM 2025-09-16T21:44:28.465Z       3d8cb49f-ec3f-4333-b08f-a1d00fe4acd1    INFO    stuff body {"message":"pong"}
```

And llrt logs:

```
[/aws/lambda/PongFn] 11:46:12 PM 2025-09-16T21:46:12.666Z       4b0c038b-f2c2-403a-9bfc-517b43eff52d    INFO    stuff {
  stuff: Response {
    headers: Headers {},
    bodyUsed: false,
    body: undefined,
    url: '',
    redirected: false,
    ok: true,
    statusText: 'OK',
    status: 200,
    type: 'basic',

}
[/aws/lambda/PongFn] 11:46:12 PM 2025-09-16T21:46:12.666Z       4b0c038b-f2c2-403a-9bfc-517b43eff52d    INFO    stuff body [object Object]
```

There's a delta in `statusText`, `Content-Type` header and `body`.  Should [Response.json](https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/blob/1a1e7cf701e505cdd9ec0b2ec0dcd3b18b90be4b/modules/llrt_fetch/src/response.rs#L303) be setting the `Content-Type` header, stringifying the output and returning a `String`? As is it looks like `Value<'js>` is just using the default to_string method.

title: ReferenceError: Error resolving module 'string_decoder/'
body:
When we try to load a package, we get the following error. It works fine in other runtimes.

```javascript
// reproduction.js
const a = require('middy/middlewares');
console.log(a);
```

```
% llrt reproduction.js
ReferenceError: Error resolving module 'string_decoder/' from '/Users/shinya/Workspaces/llrt-test/stream'
  at <anonymous> (stream:2:34145)
      at <anonymous> (stream:1:505)
      at <anonymous> (stream:2:63247)
      at <anonymous> (stream:1:505)
      at <anonymous> (stream:2:66785)
      at <anonymous> (stream:1:505)
      at <anonymous> (stream:2:71321)
      at <anonymous> (stream:1:505)
      at <anonymous> (stream:2:73688)
      at <anonymous> (stream:1:505)
```

In LLRT, the node-compatible stream uses the `readable-stream` polyfill, but the following command in it seems to be the problem.

```javascript
const { StringDecoder } = require('string_decoder/')
```

After some research, it appears that this method of adding a "/" at the end is no longer recommended. One way to avoid this is to remove the trailing "/" within the `require`.

NOTE: Before LLRT implemented `string_decoder`, esbuild may have bundled the `string_decoder` package and worked fine.

title: TLS support
body:
LLRT is a fantastic project, I can't wait to incorporate it into my projects.

However, it's currently unusable for any real-world use due to the lack of TLS support.
Without TLS, you can't interact with many external services at the moment, such as some databases.

At the moment the error I'm getting is:
`ReferenceError: Error resolving module 'tls'`

Is there an ETA for TLS support?
author: ldragone

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body:
Thanks so much for the kind words and for giving LLRT a try! 🙏

You’re right, the lack of TLS support can be a limitation for many use cases. TLS is a pretty complex module with lots of edge cases, so it will take some time and care to implement properly. We don’t have an ETA yet, but it’s definitely something we want to support.

As a workaround in the meantime, you might be able to use something like `sclient` to handle the TLS handshake externally and pass plain traffic through to LLRT?

I wasn't aware of this option with sclient.
I'll do some testing while I wait for LLRT to support TLS.

title: [bug]: "Special numeric value 0 is not allowed" error with DynamoDBDocumentClient when marshalling a nested object containing the number 0
author: namse

comments.author: namse
comments.body: No error on darwin arm64 version, error occur on linux arm64

comments.author: namse
comments.body:
# Root Cause Analysis

I've identified the root cause of this issue. The problem occurs only in Linux builds due to a compatibility issue between QuickJS and musl libc.

## Key Findings

1. **The bug**: `Number` objects (created with `new Number()`) return an empty string when calling `toString()` on Linux LLRT builds:
   ```javascript
   new Number(0).toString()   // Returns: "" (bug)
   new Number(42).toString()  // Returns: "" (bug)
   (0).toString()            // Returns: "0" (works)
   ```

2. **Platform-specific**: 
   - Linux builds use `musl` libc (`x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`)
   - macOS builds use Darwin libc (`x86_64-apple-darwin`)
   - The issue only occurs with musl libc

3. **Root cause**: QuickJS's `js_dtoa` function (which converts doubles to strings) appears to be incompatible with musl libc's floating-point string conversion implementation. The function returns an empty string instead of the number's string representation.

4. **Evidence**:
   - `Number.prototype.toString.length` is 0 on Linux (should be 1)
   - `Number.prototype.toString.name` is "" on Linux (should be "toString")
   - Other number methods (`toFixed()`, `toExponential()`) work correctly
   - String concatenation works because it uses `valueOf()`: `"" + new Number(0)` returns "0"

## Why AWS SDK fails

The AWS SDK's `@aws-sdk/util-dynamodb` package validates numbers using:
```javascript
if ([Number.NaN, Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY, Number.NEGATIVE_INFINITY]
    .map((val) => val.toString())
    .includes(num.toString())) {
    throw new Error(`Special numeric value ${num.toString()} is not allowed`);
}
```

When `num` is a Number object, `num.toString()` returns "", causing the confusing error message.

## Workaround

Until this is fixed, avoid using Number objects:
```javascript
// Don't use:
const value = new Number(0);

// Use primitive numbers instead:
const value = 0;
```

## Suggested Fix

The issue appears to be in QuickJS's number-to-string conversion when compiled with musl libc. The `js_dtoa` function needs to be made compatible with musl's libc implementation.

title: llrt 0.6.0-beta broken in container: Illegal instruction (core dumped)
body:
llrt is a very interesting project. Thank you for creating it!

Version 0.6.0 seems to introduce a bug when running llrt in a container. When used together with e.g. the busybox container, calling the 0.6.0 binary will result in `Illegal instruction (core dumped)`.
This was not the case in 0.5.1.

### Reproduction

Dockerfile
```Dockerfile
FROM busybox
ARG VERSION=v0.6.0
ADD --chmod=555 https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/releases/download/${VERSION}-beta/llrt-container-x64 /usr/bin/llrt
CMD [ "llrt", "--version" ]
```

1. Save above Dockerfile
2. In the directory of the Dockerfile run `docker build -t llrt-0.6.0 . && docker run --rm -it llrt-0.6.0 sh`
3. Input `llrt` (or `llrt --version`) and press enter

Note that calling `docker run --rm -it llrt-0.6.0` will just silently fail.

Working version with 0.5.1: `docker build --build-arg VERSION=v0.5.1 -t llrt-0.5.1 . && docker run --rm -it llrt-0.5.1`

title: Feasibility Study: Migrating LLRT from QuickJS to PrimJS Engine
body:
The recently released Lynx framework demonstrates an alternative approach to cross-platform development. Their optimized JavaScript engine PrimJS (https://github.com/lynx-family/primjs), based on QuickJS, outperforms the original QuickJS. It features improved memory management, reduced risk of memory leaks, and supports code debugging—significantly elevating QuickJS as a whole.

Is LLRT interested in exploring and evaluating this engine? If deemed suitable, could LLRT consider replacing its current QuickJS engine with PrimJS to further enhance overall performance?

I believe this would be a valuable improvement.
author: lanbomo

comments.author: Waldenesque
comments.body:
For reference...

Lynx is more or less an alternative to React Native or Flutter that's partially agnostic to frontend framework and rendering platform, developed entirely in-house and used in production by ByteDance (TikTok), which was open-sourced a few months ago. However, from comments on Hacker News it sounds like even within ByteDance this is still somewhat new and niche technology that is not actually used or even known all that widely yet. More specifically regarding their PrimJS JavaScript engine...

The whole appeal of QuickJS in the first place is being minimal and easily embeddable by consisting of a few pure C files with no external dependencies and just a makefile to build. Also even the original Bellard branch supports most of the ES2023 spec. The QuickJS-NG fork is getting ongoing development, and changed its build system to CMake and supports MSVC for Windows, but it's still a small C project approximately resembling the original upstream.

PrimJS claims to be "built on top of QuickJS" which is true in a sense, but they also claim ES2019 support which suggests they originally forked QuickJS several years back. More importantly, they have diverged radically since then. It's now a C++ project using Chromium's GN & Ninja build system, including an alternative custom interpreter partially implemented in assembly, as well as an alternative custom tracing garbage collector with stated goals of memory usage not exceeding V8 and pause time not exceeding 30 ms. And for all this at present they only claim a 28% Octane improvement.

In other words, "right tool for the job" and all that...

comments.author: lanbomo
comments.body:
@Waldenesque You make a valid point. I've noticed the performance improvements in PrimJS and ran a quick test myself—it does run faster than the original QuickJS. This made me think: Wouldn't it be great to leverage this for LLRT to boost its performance?

I'm simply proposing a feasibility study. If these enhancements could be applied to LLRT, improving its runtime performance, it would represent significant progress. This could help address its slower execution—faster speed is always better, after all.

Of course, this is just a suggestion for initial exploration. Whether PrimJS is suitable for LLRT or can be practically implemented requires proper research and testing.

My hope is simply for LLRT to become even better.

comments.author: ahaoboy
comments.body:
> [@Waldenesque](https://github.com/Waldenesque) You make a valid point. I've noticed the performance improvements in PrimJS and ran a quick test myself—it does run faster than the original QuickJS.  

How did you test it? As far as I remember, the speed difference was not that big.

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body:
@lanbomo @Waldenesque Thank you all for the interesting discussion around PrimJS. Let me share our perspective on this suggestion:

LLRT’s core philosophy prioritizes simplicity and maintainability, which is why QuickJS’s minimal, pure C implementation has been a good match for our goals. While PrimJS introduces some notable performance improvements, it also comes with significant architectural changes, such as a C++ codebase, Chromium’s GN/Ninja build system, and a custom interpreter with assembly code. These changes would introduce complexity that may not align well with our lightweight and serverless focus (also rust doesn't play so well with c++ code bases)

The 28% Octane improvement is impressive, but we need to weigh it against the added build and maintenance overhead, as well as the likely increase in runtime footprint. These factors are especially important given our constraints and long-term maintainability goals.

At the moment, we’re actively using the QuickJS-NG project, which continues to evolve while preserving compatibility with our architecture. Our current focus is on optimizing LLRT’s core functionality within its existing design.

As @ahaoboy mentioned, we would also want to see performance benchmarks in real-world use cases, not just synthetic metrics, to better evaluate the potential trade-offs.

Overall, while we recognize and appreciate the innovations in PrimJS, we believe that continuing with QuickJS-NG offers the best balance of performance, stability, and simplicity for LLRT at this time. We’ll continue to monitor developments in PrimJS and are open to specific proposals that align well with our design approach.

P.S.
`From a performance standpoint, there is a ceiling with fully interpreted runtimes. Even a basic JIT could unlock far greater gains than a 28% improvement on Octane. There’s also potential in transitioning QuickJS to a register-based VM, which could reduce stack overhead and better support future JIT work. For those interested, there’s more discussion on this here: https://github.com/quickjs-ng/quickjs/issues/659`

comments.author: lanbomo
comments.body: @richarddavison Thanks for your reply. Indeed, the balance among performance, stability, and simplicity is important, and the QuickJS-NG project is continuously evolving—it will surely deliver even better results in the future. I currently have no further questions, and I trust that the professionalism and rigor of the core team will make LLRT even better. Thank you.

title: Date.now().toString(16).length returns a string length of 23
body:
When performing toString(16) on a number whose length exceeds 32 bits, the string returned is longer than usual, and the invalid length is filled with `String.fromCharCode(0)`.

For example, if you run the following program:
~~~js
const d = Date.now().toString(16);
console.log(d)
console.log(d.length)
console.log(d[11] == String.fromCharCode(0))
console.log(d[11] == undefined)
console.log(Buffer.from(d));
~~~

~~~
19747d23cce
23
true
false

comments.author: Jarred-Sumner
comments.body: I don't know a ton about LLRT so I can't really comment on performance differences between Bun and LLRT (is LLRT JIT'd?) , but @weklund if you guys run into any issues with Bun or have any questions am happy to hop on a call or do a shared slack/discord workspace - feel free to email jarred@bun.sh

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body:
Hey @Jarred-Sumner @weklund, thanks for your comments! Happy to provide some clarity here.

LLRT was designed with a very specific use case in mind, and it's not intended to compete directly with Bun (or Node/Deno), rather to complement them. In fact, for many traditional server-side workloads or computationally intensive JavaScript, Bun’s performance, thanks to its use of a highly optimized JIT engine and native implementations going to be significantly better. That’s a major strength of Bun and one of the reasons it’s such a compelling runtime for a broad range of use cases.

LLRT takes a different approach. It’s built on QuickJS, a smaller, interpreter-based engine, and implements a much more limited API surface, however intentionally so. This minimalism is actually a benefit in serverless environments, where cold start time and runtime size can have a major impact on user experience. LLRT’s focus is on fast startup, small footprint (<5MB executable), and just enough functionality to make it useful for a lot of things, such as data transformations or API orchestration in environments like AWS Lambda.

So while it's not an apples-to-apples comparison, it can be useful benchmarking LLRT and Bun for YOUR specific use case. Especially if those are aligned with serverless workloads. I’d be more than happy to support that effort you have any questions or issues :)

comments.author: o-alexandrov
comments.body:
Using ARM 1024MB RAM, Bun (same for Deno) has almost 3x slower cold start ~304ms than provided by AWS Node.js 22 runtime ~135ms. On a side note, LLRT got almost 2x slower (compared to initial ~1yr ago LLRT numbers ~20ms, now ~40ms) due to continuous size increments. But LLRT is still not provided by AWS, meaning we should compare it to Bun, not Node.js, and there’s almost 8x difference between the two. There is an option to [llrt compile](https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/issues/110#issuecomment-1935467330) to bytecode the source code for LLRT, but Maxday’s benchmark doesn’t have it. (Bun also has [—bytecode](https://bun.sh/docs/bundler/executables#bytecode-compilation) but it cannot come close given the existing difference)
https://maxday.github.io/lambda-perf/

It’s impossible for Bun to compete with a provided runtime due to caching, etc. whereas Docker’ized (Deno in their blog like to compare performance in Docker environments) Lambda functions are much slower than provided + Lambda Layers.

The above means there’s no place for Bun/Deno in AWS Lambda, until they convince AWS to offer them as AWS provided runtimes. Cold starts aside, Lambda processes one request at a time, so there’s no real-world performance benefit between Node.js and Bun, whereas there are major stability differences between the two

title: Further improving the footprint
body:
LLRT already has features that other runtimes do not have, but we believe that we need to further refine them, even if we have to forego some compatibility.

To further improve the small footprint, one of the features of this product, we are considering the following:

- llrt_fetch: Keep http2 support as a crate, but default LLRT to http1 only (this will prevent the `h2` crate from being included)
- llrt_fetch: By adopting `rustls-platform-verifier` instead of `webkpi-roots`, certificates are not stored internally. See also https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/issues/768#issuecomment-2930897137
- llrt_fetch/llrt_zlib: The crate will retain brotli functionality, but will not use it as an LLRT. I think it won't be a problem as long as it supports zstd, which is used for other purposes and is indispensable, and gzip, which is still widely used. https://w3techs.com/technologies/details/ce-compression
- llrt_os: We'll put all the functions the `sysinfo` crate needs behind the feature flags and change the default to off.
- llrt_crypto: Organizing crates required for subtleCrypto (this requires improvements to the crate it uses).

Is there anything else you can think of?

title: Symbol.toStringTag is missing in Web API object instances
body:
An appropriate `Symbol.toStringTag` is missing from all Web Platform API objects such as Response, CryptoKey, and others.

This symbol is widely used to deal with detecting the input's type without relying on globals and instanceof checks, especially when it comes to executing on varied js runtimes with, sometimes, polyfills in place.

```js
const key = await crypto.subtle.generateKey({ name: 'HMAC', hash: 'SHA-256' }, false, ['sign', 'verify'])
key[Symbol.toStringTag] === 'CryptoKey' // expect true, got false on v0.5.1-beta
```

```js
const response = Response.json({})
response[Symbol.toStringTag] === 'Response' // expect true, got false on v0.5.1-beta
```

title: The execution order of asynchronous processes differs from other runtimes
author: nabetti1720

comments.author: nabetti1720
comments.body:
The reason I couldn't run `setImmediate()` in Deno was simply because I was using an old version of Deno. I was able to run it by `import { setImmediate } from "node:timers";`, so I've pasted the results here.

Deno : 
```
% deno run blockingTimer.js
🦖 [1] MAINLINE: Sync process: start
🦖 [2] MAINLINE: Sync process: timer exit after 2000
🦖 [3] MAINLINE: Sync process: end
👶 [4] MICRO: queueMicrotask
⏰ [6] TIMER: setTimeout[0ms] finished
👨 [5] MACRO: setImmediate
⏰ [7] TIMER: setTimeout[500ms] finished
⏰ [8] TIMER: setTimeout[1000ms] finished
```

This behavior can be explained if we consider Deno's `setImmediate(fn)` to be internally the same as `setTimeout(fn, 0)`.

comments.author: nabetti1720
comments.body:
A while ago, DelSkayn explained quickjs's microtasks in another issue.

https://github.com/DelSkayn/rquickjs/issues/351#issuecomment-2742994628

> QuickJS by default only has micro-tasks. If I remember the terms correctly micro-tasks are promises and suchs and macros-tasks are incoming events like in the browser click events and setTimeout. QuickJS does not implement setTimeout or any functionality which results in events like IO so there are no macro tasks.

Reading this comment, I think it's highly impractical to have a macro task queue below the rquickjs/quickjs layer. On the other hand, If it were possible to address the other issue of timer order control, it may be possible to improve behavior with the following implementation.

- For setImmediate tasks, register the task as a timer task with the timeout time negative (i.e., treat it as having ended in the past/for example, the date and time of the first commit with LLRT).

It's not exactly the same as setImmediate control by the nodejs's check phase, but I think there's a possibility that it will be able to behave more like it now.

title: Fetch does not support webstreams
body:
Currently, fetch only support reading entire responses and requests from and into memory.
The streaming API's of Request and Response is not implemented.
Since the introduction of native streaming API's by @jackkleeman this functionality is now possible.
Spec is here:
https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#body
`body` should return a ReadableStream.

Currently we return `null`:
https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/blob/38af49052380ce2e1dd4b5bc1b93ce3771eba572/modules/llrt_http/src/response.rs#L316

title: Zstd compression/decompression support in the zlib module
body:
In node.js 23.8.0, the zlib module added the following convenience methods:

[zlib.zstdCompress(buffer[, options], callback)](https://nodejs.org/api/zlib.html#zlibzstdcompressbuffer-options-callback)
[zlib.zstdCompressSync(buffer[, options])](https://nodejs.org/api/zlib.html#zlibzstdcompresssyncbuffer-options)
[zlib.zstdDecompress(buffer[, options], callback)](https://nodejs.org/api/zlib.html#zlibzstddecompressbuffer-options-callback)
[zlib.zstdDecompressSync(buffer[, options])](https://nodejs.org/api/zlib.html#zlibzstddecompresssyncbuffer-options)

In #523, we proposed implementing it when we added new support for the zlib module, but it was removed in order to prioritize compatibility with node.js.(https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/pull/523/commits/09211908c52742ce272fe1a3101ee4ef4a35621a)

If we refer to this implementation, I think it won't be too difficult to support it with LLRT. I would like to prioritize other issues, so I hope someone will respond. :)

body:
In the [latest commit](https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/commit/369a345edbad8cdd2ba22e40b62d77bee36e0697), when I try to load the following npm package, it crashes:

```javascript
// reproduction.js
const a = require('pg');
console.log(a);
```

```
% LLRT_LOG=trace llrt reproduction.js
... Omit the middle part...
2025-03-16T23:04:54.247Z TRACE llrt_core::module_loader::require: After specifier: __cjs:/Users/shinya/Workspaces/llrt-test/node_modules/pg/lib/native/index.js 
zsh: trace trap  LLRT_LOG=trace llrt reproduction.js
```

The final trace is output in the following location, but the existing traces do not identify the cause.
https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/blob/369a345edbad8cdd2ba22e40b62d77bee36e0697/llrt_core/src/module_loader/require.rs#L125-L128

Therefore, we ran the program with tracing for each step and found the cause of the problem.
```rust
trace!("After specifier: {}", import_specifier);

trace!("1");
let binding = ctx.userdata::<RefCell<RequireState>>().unwrap();
trace!("2");
let mut state = binding.borrow_mut();
trace!("3");
```

Execution result:
```
% LLRT_LOG=trace llrt reproduction.js
... Omit the middle part...
2025-03-16T23:04:54.247Z TRACE llrt_core::module_loader::resolver: +- Resolved by `LOAD_AS_DIRECTORY`: /Users/shinya/Workspaces/llrt-test/node_modules/pg/lib/native/index.js

2025-03-16T23:04:54.247Z TRACE llrt_core::module_loader::require: 1 
2025-03-16T23:04:54.247Z TRACE llrt_core::module_loader::require: 2 
zsh: trace trap  LLRT_LOG=trace llrt reproduction.js
```

Possible cause location:
```rust
let mut state = binding.borrow_mut();
```

I don't know why this command causes a crash when the previous `unwrap()` doesn't.

@richarddavison and everyone, Are there any possible reasons?

title: Reduce number of dependencies of llrt_crypto
body:
The module has too many dependencies, it really pollutes any project trying to import it since some have very deep web of dependencies. For example we pull in two different bigint implementations (`num-bigint-dig` and `crypto-bigint`)
We have a lot of duplicate with ring anyway and we should prefer using it. Curve crypto is still not in ring, but planned (https://github.com/briansmith/ring/issues/1771)
author: Sytten

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body:
I shared your concern @Sytten when starting the crypto refactor derived from @nabetti1720 fantastic ground work. Problem with ring is that it only supports a fraction of the crypto APIs/algos we need. Even if ring has support for an algorithm, it only supports decryption/verification and not encryption/signature etc.
That being said, we should provide different web crypto implementations:
- One with pure Rust implementations: using the current crates
- Another one with system: OpenSSL/LibreSSL/BoringSSL

comments.author: Sytten
comments.body: We might want to look at graviola (https://crates.io/crates/graviola) made by a maintainer of rustls.

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body:
That would be great. Unfortunately we can't get rid of everything as graviolia/ring/aws-lc only supports some of the operations we need in subtle crypto. I don't think there is plans to support full API either:
https://github.com/briansmith/ring/issues/691
To my recollection aws-lc-rs also only exposes the same APIs as ring and does not have bindings for the full lib crypto APIs. Otherwise that would be an option.

title: Execute TypeScript files that contains only erasable TypeScript syntax
body:
I understand that LLRT is not aiming to fully transpile TypeScript.

But I think supporting the execution of TypeScript files that only contain erasable TypeScript syntax (type definitions) would help increase the use cases of LLRT.

For reference:
https://nodejs.org/api/typescript.html#type-stripping

Things to do:
- Supporting new extensions in custom resolver (*.ts, *.mts, *.cts)
- Remove type definitions (Replace with whitespace using regular expression?)
- Cache code with removed type definitions (for reuse)
author: nabetti1720

comments.author: ahaoboy
comments.body:
https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/issues/692

I had the same idea before, but due to size considerations, llrt may not support it. Ideally, this function should be implemented by supporting custom loaders, and it can be part of the rquickjs ecosystem similar to llrt_modules.

comments.author: nabetti1720
comments.body: Yes. As you say, we think that introducing a high-function transpiler like `swc` is not appropriate because it would increase the footprint. Here, we thought that we could start limited support for TypeScript by simply removing type definitions (as we do with node.js).

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body:
This is the direction most runtimes are going for. We realize that this improves user experience but comes with a cost, it's bad for performance.
Reason being that there is an additional step required where we need to parse the JS sources and removing types before loading them in the JavaScript engine. You will pay this penalty for every file being loaded.
It also kind of incentivizes shipping raw Typescript sources instead of creating a production, single JS bundle which is what's recommended, particularly in Serverless environments. Same principle should be applied for Node really.

Currently the biggest use-case preventing me from using LLRT with more of my lambda's is the missing Intl library. I actually don't need any localization, I just need to be able to use a library like dayjs and convert a date into the appropriate timezone and perform common operations like startOf('day')
Here is an example.
```
import dayjs from 'dayjs';
import timezone from 'dayjs/plugin/timezone';

const date3 = dayjs('2022-03-02T15:45:34Z').tz('America/Denver').startOf('day');

console.log(date3.toISOString()); //2022-03-02T07:00:00.000Z

Pretty much every date library I've looked at just uses Intl under the hood to perform this type of operation.

Let me know if you have any guidance for this use-case.

title: ENHANCEMENT: Standalone executable compile option for local machines
body:
LLRT, as many have already noticed, is the smallest JavaScript runtime implementing the largest number of Node.js APIs and WinterCG proposals. Major runtimes like Bun and Deno approach feature completeness and Node.js compatibility, but none match LLRT's current usable feature set within such a small footprint.

Standalone executables weren't part of LLRT's initial design. However, its local binaries (i.e. non-Lambda and non-Container) work effectively as a JavaScript CLI runtime and REPL. This is unsurprising, given that the underlying QuickJS engine provides these features and the option to compile standalone executables.

Just look at the current standalone executable sizes between Bun, Deno, and LLRT (LLRT + bytecode size, hypothetical)

| Windows x64 Runtime                    | Standalone Executable Size |
|----------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Bun                                    | 107 MB                     |
| Deno                                   | 81 MB                      |
| LLRT + bytecode                        | 9 MB                       |
| LLRT, upx -9 --ultra-brute, + bytecode | 3 MB                       |

Here are some of the use cases for a tiny standalone executable runtime:
- rapid prototyping of CLI programs
- distribution of development prototypes
- teaching JavaScript in K-12, without the burden of the whole package management ecosystem
- alternative to Python or Bash scripting for day-to-day administration task
- game development

comments.author: ahaoboy
comments.body:
tjs is also a very small js runtime

llrt's small size and rust's cross-platform compilation also make it very suitable for running some dynamic scripts in resource-constrained environments such as embedded systems and routers. These devices usually have only 50mb of storage space.


https://github.com/saghul/txiki.js

https://github.com/ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark

@darcyclarke @jasongodev Not quite sure what you mean by "Standalone executable compile option".
Something like `llrt --compile --target arm64 bundle.js -o llrt-executable`?

comments.author: darcyclarke
comments.body:
@richarddavison yes, something like what you shared would be ideal. 

If it's not clear, we want the program compiled _with_ the runtime. Today, `llrt compile` only produces an optimized program meaning that you still have to have `llrt` somewhere on your system. 

As @jasongodev pointed out, `bun`, `deno` & even `node`<sup>\*WIP</sup> have this ability to bundle/compile the runtime & program together but the size is massive compared to what `llrt` could produce. If you added this, I could see many dev tools implementing their CLIs with `llrt` as it would massively shrink their package distributions as well as have comparative if not better performance to `bun` (at least in the benchmarks I've run on short-lived tasks - again, the ideal for dev tools/CLI use-cases).

I know that today `llrt` distributes itself as a target-specific binary so it may be a big ask for cross-compilation (not sure). That said, it would be nice to default generate all known/supported targets with some kind of common target prefix/suffix & be able to pass one or many targets to overwrite that default (ie. let me run `llrt --compile` once with the right config instead of `n` times & in `n` envs to generate all required targets). 

Afaik right now the relevant supported targets would be:

- `darwin-arm64`
- `darwin-x64`
- `linux-arm64`
- `linux-x64`
- `windows-x64`

> Note: I believe the `container` & `lambda` targets are specific to hosted envs (not sure what's different about them) which I might suggest not making part of a default target set for this.

refs. https://bun.sh/docs/bundler/executables, https://docs.deno.com/runtime/reference/cli/compile/ & https://nodejs.org/api/single-executable-applications.html

P.S. I feel like you could reuse the existing `llrt compile` command & just add a flag like `--with-runtime` or `--executable` as a non-breaking change & the expected output would be the program with the runtime you're using in that moment. This would get us 90% the way there without nice defaults/cross-compilation which I imagine could take much longer to support.

title: `Buffer.from(str, "base64")` fails for URL safe base64 encoded strings
body:
When executing the following:

```javascript
// buffer.test.js

const str = "eyJodHRwczovL2F2YXRhcnMuZ2l0aHVidXNlcmNvbnRlbnQuY29tL3UvODk1MTgwOTU_dj00In0";

const buffer = Buffer.from(str, "base64");

console.log(buffer.toString());
```

With Node I get:

```
$ node test/buffer.test.js
{"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/89518095?v=4"}
```

With LLRT I get:

```
$ ./llrt test/buffer.test.js           
Error: Base64Error
  at <anonymous> (/.../packages/lambda/test/buffer.test.js:3:23)
```

If I replace the `_` in `str` with `/` then it decodes the base64 string successfully in both Node and LLRT.

Node decodes both standard and URL safe base64 encoded strings, but LLRT only supports the standard charset at the moment as it uses the [`forgiving_decode_to_vec`](https://docs.rs/base64-simd/latest/base64_simd/fn.forgiving_decode_to_vec.html) function [here](https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/blob/main/libs/llrt_encoding/src/lib.rs#L141) which only supports the standard charset.
author: ainsleyrutterford

comments.author: ainsleyrutterford
comments.body:
Could LLRT first check which charset is being decoded by looking for the `+/` or `-_` characters, and then decode the string using the corresponding charset? That doesn't solve the problem of `forgiving_decode_to_vec` only supporting the standard charset though :/

Or I guess simply replacing instances of `-_` with `+/` before using `forgiving_decode_to_vec` might be sufficient?

title: Strategies to keep the runtime light?
body:
I don't know how much Node's (or llrt's - I mention Node because obviously, one stumbles across this when looking for a lightweight alternative) size has increased due to including features that maybe could've been released separately but I found it concerning that you're also e.g. including a test runner already. 

Are there plans to either release runtimes that are to be used for production only and don't contain things like said test runner and possibly other features only needed during development? Or maybe the ability to create custom runtimes that don't include them? Or does the footprint of the engine make up so much of the runtime that anything that could be reasonably excluded is negligible?
author: s-h-a-d-o-w

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body:
Hey @s-h-a-d-o-w. Thanks for that comment. Keeping the runtime light has always been a top priority for LLRT. It's crucial that we keep things as tight as possible to reduce both memory footprint and improve startup times. A lot of effort has been put into keeping things as slim as possible. One example of this is that we only support a low number of encodings, and try to opt out of dependencies adding to much we don't need. Another one is that we pack the entire executable in a zstd compressed self-extracting executable to improve startup and reduce size on Lambda. Rust does a pretty good job of removing unwanted stuff at compile time using  DCE (dead code elimination), LTO (link time optimization) and minification. However there is a always a constant balance between features, size and performance.

As we also prioritize performance we unfortunately put on some weight. For example we use opt-level 3 (or -O3) when compiling release binaries which causes some monomorphization, loop unrolling and a lot of function inlining. All these increases performance but significantly increases size as well.

The engine itself, quickjs-ng, weights in about 1mb. On top of that there are a lot of things that are quite bulky in Rust projects we can't get away from. I'll attaching a list of biggest size contributors F.Y.I:
[llrt-bloat.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18353030/llrt-bloat.txt)

As you can see there are many things that add size other than the engine such as Rust standard library, Tokio asynchronous runtime, tls/certificates/encryption (ring, rustls, webpki), certificates, compression algorithms (zstd, brotli, deflate), http client and protocols (hyper, h2) etc.

As the current strategy of LLRT is to be WinterCG there are still a few things missing (webstreams etc). We have tought about somehow modularizing even further by building shared libraries for each LLRT module and load them at runtime. Users can then just remove the shared libraries they don't want and the core will be 10x smaller. The tricky part with that is it requires a lot of effort and Rust doesn't have a stable ABI so introduces a whole heap of problems and is not being considered at the moment.

That being said with this new modular approach you can build your own runtime "just" including what you need. Most of the runtime components is moved to separate crates.

comments.author: s-h-a-d-o-w
comments.body: Unfortunate that modularity isn't feasible but thanks a lot for this thorough explanation!

title: `.toString()` of 0 returns empty string for some radix values
body:
In Node, `(0).toString(16)` returns `"0"`, whereas in LLRT it returns `""`.

Depending on the radix value used, the behaviour differs slightly, LLRT sometimes matches the Node implementation:

```js
(0).toString(2);  // Node: "0", LLRT: "0"
(0).toString(10); // Node: "0", LLRT: "0"
(0).toString(16); // Node: "0", LLRT: ""
(0).toString(13); // Node: "0", LLRT: ""
```

This causes issues when using dependencies like https://github.com/kjur/jsrsasign (which I'm just using until https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/issues/184 is implemented which will hopefully allow us to use https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken).

title: Can't import CJS modules via ESM import statement
body:
While verifying the loading of the Node.js package, we encountered another strange event.

```javascript
// logger.js
import { Logger } from '@aws-lambda-powertools/logger'
const logger = new Logger()
logger.info('Hello world')
```
```
% llrt logger.js 
SyntaxError: Could not find export 'default' in module '/Users/shinya/Workspaces/llrt-test/node_modules/lodash.merge/./index.js'
  at <anonymous> (eval_script:1:5)

% node logger.js 
{"level":"INFO","message":"Hello world","sampling_rate":0,"service":"service_undefined","timestamp":"2024-10-22T13:47:00.450Z"}

% bun logger.js 
{"level":"INFO","message":"Hello world","sampling_rate":0,"service":"service_undefined","timestamp":"2024-10-22T13:50:09.638Z"}
```

While investigating reproduction methods, we found that the same event reproduced itself in the following application structure.

```javascript
// hello.js
var hello = function world() {
  return "hello world"
}
module.exports = hello;
```
```javascript
// main.js
import hello from './hello.js'
console.log(hello())
```

```
% llrt main.js
SyntaxError: Could not find export 'default' in module '/Users/shinya/Workspaces/llrt-test/./hello.js'
  at <anonymous> (eval_script:1:5)

% node main.js  
file:///Users/shinya/Workspaces/llrt-test/main.js:1
import hello from './hello.js'
       ^^^^^
SyntaxError: The requested module './hello.js' does not provide an export named 'default'
    at ModuleJob._instantiate (node:internal/modules/esm/module_job:171:21)
    at async ModuleJob.run (node:internal/modules/esm/module_job:254:5)
    at async onImport.tracePromise.__proto__ (node:internal/modules/esm/loader:483:26)
    at async asyncRunEntryPointWithESMLoader (node:internal/modules/run_main:117:5)

Node.js v22.9.0

% bun main.js 
hello world
```

The same event occurs with Node.js in this way. However, the behavior changes when `hello.js` is changed to `hello.cjs`.

```javascript
// main.js
import hello from './hello.cjs' // The content is exactly the same as hello.js
console.log(hello())
```

```
% llrt main.js 
SyntaxError: Could not find export 'default' in module '/Users/shinya/Workspaces/llrt-test/./hello.cjs'
  at <anonymous> (eval_script:1:5)

% node main.js 
hello world

% bun main.js 
hello world
```

The following is what we can assume from these findings:
- Bun has the ability to import CJS files.
- Node.js has the ability to import CJS files with the help of package definitions or extensions.
- LLRT does not support either.
author: nabetti1720

comments.author: richarddavison

I've tested an approach where we detect inside the loader if we should resolve a CJS module and then generate a source file which internally uses our require function to then re-export that. This proved to be more difficult due to cyclic issues as we won't run the loader again which is inside the require code. I need to think about a different approach to this problem.

comments.author: nabetti1720
comments.body:
My understanding is that the current implementation is correct because I believe that the extension inherently contains information to determine if it is a CJS or an ESM.

But since these use cases work in other runtimes, I believe that other runtimes implement more complex logic than the determination by extension.

I think LLRT should first have an option (e.g., an environment variable) to temporarily cancel the strict decision to accommodate these use cases, while keeping the existing implementation as much as possible. Then I can enable that option and continue the validation.

After that, we believe a better approach would be to implement an automatic decision-making process.

EDIT: I have found the following section to control this. If `LLRT_IGNORE_CJS_CHECK=1`, we believe we can further include js and mjs files in the condition so that it works as expected. 

https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/blob/d18dcf3f897f793aa026c18b90c9277cf4e3bc8f/llrt_core/src/module_loader/loader.rs#L151-L154

If I am correct in the points I have found, I would like to raise a PR, is that a problem?

NOTE: I also like the idea of a cjs extension check only if `LLRT_STRICT_CJS_REQUIRE=1`. Is this preferable?

title: New bundle type for AWS-friendly web applications
body: We thought we could create a new Web Application Stack around LLRT that is compliant with standard Web APIs (in other words, not too dependent on the Node.js API), highly scalable and compatible with AWS. We would like to call it the `hola` web application stack. Incidentally, `hola (pronounced /ˈola/)` means 'Hi' or hello' in Spanish :) The components are as follows : - H : Hono - O : Drizzle ORM - L : AWS Lambda on LLRT - A : Amazon Aurora Serverless v2(with AWS Data API) **1. Hono** <[Website](https://hono.dev/)> <[Github](https://github.com/honojs/hono)> - It has a UX similar to express, but uses only the standard WebAPI. It consists of a small core and a lot of middleware, and development is very active. - In addition, there is an adapter called `hono/aws-lambda` that provides a mechanism to wrap the Request/Response to interact with the API Gateway and ALB (https://hono.dev/docs/getting-started/aws-lambda). **2. Drizzle ORM** <[Website](https://orm.drizzle.team/)> <[Github](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm)> - Like Prisma, it supports a variety of databases, but most importantly, it works with `@aws-sdk/client-rds-data` and supports the AWS Data API (https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/get-started-postgresql#aws-data-api). To add, it is worth noting that these products are not dependent on other packages. I have already been able to get my lambda to work by bundling the additional modules needed by the following sources into the `full-sdk` (when actually creating the new bundle type, the number of `@aws-sdk`'s should be narrowed down to the minimum necessary). Again, in the example below, I only need a single `index.mjs` to create a web application that is highly compatible with AWS managed services. ```javascript // index.mjs import { Hono } from 'hono' import { handle } from 'hono/aws-lambda' import { sql } from 'drizzle-orm' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/aws-data-api/pg' import { RDSDataClient } from '@aws-sdk/client-rds-data' const rdsClient = new RDSDataClient({}) const db = drizzle(rdsClient, { database: process.env['DATABASE'], secretArn: process.env['SECRET_ARN'], resourceArn: process.env['RESOURCE_ARN'], }) const app = new Hono() app.post('/path/to/resource', async (c) => { const result = await db.execute(sql`SELECT tablename FROM pg_tables limit 10`) return c.json(result.rows) }) export const handler = handle(app) ``` Execution result (sorry for the Japanese display screenshot): We propose a new bundle type of `hola` to introduce a different and new use case to the LLRT world. I would be happy if you are interested. :)

title: WHATWG Streams implementation
body:
I'm fairly interested in contributing an implementation of the web stream API. As I see it there are two options:
1. Use an all JS implementation, taking inspiration from the reference implementation from the working group, using some native APIs where necessary (as I understand from https://github.com/creatorrr/web-streams-polyfill, this will be necessary)
2. Write a Rust implementation of the streams spec

I would probably lean towards doing the latter, either as a separate crate if it can be abstracted well or simply within this repo. Are there any opinions on how this should be done? Thanks!


---

- [x] Main stream implementation (#761)
- [ ] TransformStream implementation (#792)
- [ ] TextEncoderStream and TextDecoderStream implementation (#793)
author: jackkleeman

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body: Hi @jackkleeman. Thanks for considering contributing. #2 would almost be a requirement due to performance since there is no JIT in quick JS JavaScript implementation would be very slow. There is already a native rust implementation of a simple and incomplete streams API used by `child_process` module. The tricky part is that the streams API is very large, complex and contains a lot of cases so a native implementation would probably have to take some shortcuts and be not strictly compliant with Node.

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body:
> Latest update: the readable streams tests all pass, and most of the byte stream tests too. I am entering a very busy time at work so will probably take a pause for a few weeks.

Fantastic! Take your time, I've been silently keeping an eye on your fork and you've done amazing work! Hats off 🎩

comments.author: jackkleeman
comments.body:
if you are keeping an eye on it, any feedback about the horrible OwnedBorrowMut (for stream, controller and reader) mess would be appreciated. You don't realise how much the rust borrow checker does for you until you start having to grapple with its rules being enforced at runtime....
Generally my methodology has been to create the owned borrow values at the entrypoint function, and pass them down. Furthermore, you need to make sure that the borrows are released whenever you call out to user code (as they may call back in to your code), so that means basically passing them everywhere, and passing them as owned borrows, not references, because you can't release the borrow without ownership. That means you also need to pass them in to functions, consume them, and then return reborrowed values back out again, in many cases. Which leads to this incredible infectious signature: fn (stream, controller, reader, ...) -> Result<(stream, controller, reader)>. And of course, controller can generally be one of two values, and reader may be None or another two values. So its a lot of combinations!

Maybe this is unavoidable. I have considered having some sort of struct to contain all three, but due to the combinations of different readers and controllers, I don't know if this will really make things any simpler. And more generally, there is the fact that refactoring into more sensible things (eg, remove the cyclical references stream -> controller -> stream) will depart from the spec. Even now, my understanding of the end to end flow of (eg) a byte is poor simply because of the complexity, and I rely on being extremely close to the spec for things to work.

Anyway, if you have an opinion on this, id love to hear it!

comments.author: jackkleeman
comments.body:
Sidenote while its in my brain - quickjs has no arraybuffer transfer function. I have tried to think of a way to hack it on the rquickjs side, but I don't think its possible as we don't control the arraybuffer constructor and so its tricky to change the fact that it will be dropped by quickjs when the `detach` method is called. 

quickjs-ng have implemented this function. I don't think it would be hard to contribute to quickjs. For the time being we can get around it by just copying the bytes, but this may lead to some tests that don't pass, if they have ways to detect for this. Plus, it will lead to a fair few copies, because the spec really likes transferring array buffers.

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body:
> Anyway, if you have an opinion on this, id love to hear it!

Not at the moment. I would need to have a closer look at everything you've built to see how it works. 

>  quickjs has no arraybuffer transfer function

No it does not (as its an ES2024 feature) but it allows you access the raw underlying byte slice (which causes the holding ArrayBuffer to detach them). Take a look here:
https://github.com/awslabs/llrt/blob/58cf435e79b0851ed65477d430ed921628c5adbb/llrt_core/src/modules/util/text_encoder.rs#L49

comments.author: jackkleeman
comments.body: I don't think it detaches, unless I'm mistaken? You can get a slice to the bytes, but it still owns it, and when GC'd it will `free` the slice. It's not possible to cause a detach without triggering this free, as far as I can see. Hence you have to copy it to safely transfer it

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body:
> I don't think it detaches, unless I'm mistaken? You can get a slice to the bytes, but it still owns it, and when GC'd it will `free` the slice. It's not possible to cause a detach without triggering this free, as far as I can see. Hence you have to copy it to safely transfer it

title: Usage of aws-jwt-verify fails with missing "https.request" and "crypto.createPublicKey"
body:
I had a stab at using LLRT for running an API Gateway Lambda authorizer with the `aws-jwt-verify` JS lib (I'm one of the maintainers of that) in LLRT and I'd like to report my findings.

## Missing `https` module

`aws-jwt-verify` uses the Node.js "https" module which leads to an error when importing `aws-jwt-verify`:

`ReferenceError: Error resolving module 'https' from '/var/task/index.mjs'`

Interestingly you can plug other HTTP helpers into aws-jwt-verify, such as `fetch`, which at first I thought would be a solution--but it's not because the static `import { request } from "https"`, even though unused, remains in the `aws-jwt-verify` code and will trip up usage in LLRT.

Was able to overcome this with some esbuild magic, injecting a stub https module with a non implemented request function, so that the import doesn't fail (and then plugging in fetch instead).

I'm not sure what the best way forward is, but the thought did occur to me that it might be helpful for LLRT to include stubs like that for all Node.js modules, and raise `NotImplementedError` when calling not implemented functions? At least the static imports work then, and you'd only run into the `NotImplementedError` if you or the libraries you use actually use those Node.js functions.

Especially for libraries I can see that be of use, since they often do many static imports, in code paths that your code might not actually be using.

Note: aws-jwt-verify uses Node.js `https` module because it supports older Node versions (from 16 onwards) that do not have `fetch` onboard yet.

## Missing 'createPublicKey' in module 'crypto'

After solving the `https` import error I ran into: `SyntaxError: Could not find export 'createPublicKey' in module 'crypto'`

Cannot stub that out so for now my LLRT journey with `aws-jwt-verify` ends.

***

Thanks for the LLRT effort!

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body: Hi @ottokruse thanks for your comments. That's a valid concern. Crypto will reach web-crypto / subtle compliance in the future. In regards to `http` and `https` modules that's a different beast as they are heavily dependent on stream support. We have a stream stub (pulled from Node.js) but it's not ported to Rust as the API is huge. We also have a native stream implementation that doesn't have feature parity and is used for child processes. The plan right now is to add this "minimal" stream API for http and https modules in version 1.0 but right now users would have to use build tooling (such as esbuild) to replace them with empty implementations. I know this is not ideal and maybe we should provide a mechanism like you suggested to provide runtime errors at the callsite.

title: further advances in uuid compatibility
body:
We have renamed the native implementation to `llrt:uuid` to avoid conflicts with existing Node.js package names. (See also #472) 
Next, to make this native `llrt:uuid` even better (for greater compatibility with uuid packages), we believe the following features can be implemented relatively easily.

- uuid.MAX
- uuid.v1ToV6()
- uuid.V6()
- uuid.v6ToV1()
- uuid.V7()

Fortunately, the [uuid crate](https://docs.rs/uuid/1.10.0/uuid/) used by LLRT seems to be compatible with v6 and v7 generation, and the other methods and properties can be hinted at by the [node.js package implementation](https://github.com/uuidjs/uuid/tree/main/src).


We are hopeful that this feature will be picked up by someone who needs it and wants to contribute in some way to this project. :)

https://nodejs.org/api/util.html#encodings-supported-when-nodejs-is-built-with-the-small-icu-option

This would be just the task for someone who wants to contribute to this project. 👍

title: uuid implementation needs to be updated
body:
For the uuid functionality provided by [external package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/uuid?activeTab=readme) in node.js, LLRT natively implements it, which contributes to speeding up the process.

However, new methods and properties have been created in current node.js packages, making them incompatible.
A quick check shows that the following methods and properties supported since uuid@9.1 are not supported in LLRT.

- uuid.MAX
- uuid.v1ToV6()
- uuid.V6()
- uuid.v6ToV1()
- uuid.V7()

In the ESBUILD example in the README, uuid is excluded with the `--external` option, so I believe we need to aim for full compatibility.
Fortunately, the [uuid crate](https://docs.rs/uuid/1.10.0/uuid/) used by LLRT seems to be compatible with v6 and v7 generation, and the other methods and properties can be hinted at by the node.js package implementation.

title: Make URL and URLSearchParams more compliant with WHATWG URL specification
body: In trying to use the `URL` module, I quickly found that it's not compliant with the [URL standard](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/) for many normal use-cases. The first issue I came across was with the handling of the `#` for hashes (fragments) in both getting and setting the hash, so I decided to set up the [web-platform-tests for url](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/tree/b634532883c8dd54ac7ef4a29b5eccaf5125359f/url) as part of the LLRT unit test suite which uncovered a host of other issues for common web use-cases. title: Is it possible to publish common modules as third-party packages, such as rquickjs-ext similar to deno?
body: Some common modules such as os, path, fs, etc., which are not closely coupled with the runtime, can they be extracted as separate third-party libraries? For example, rquickjs-ext, so that other projects that only use rquickjs can also use it
author: ahaoboy

comments.author: richarddavison
comments.body:
It probably can! We "semi-started" to support this by moving out runtime specific code to its own crate. Right now there are a couple of blockers tho:

1 There is some lambda specific features (currently gated) that reside in `llrt_core`
2 The library depends on some JS bundled code to be present (for things like ESM), this should be moved and built into `core`
3 The core module will at compile time create a perfect hashmap and embed modules into its own executable.

I experimented with a different approach for 3 by appending a special data format that contained an index of all embedded files + the raw bytecode at the end of the executable. This proved to slightly increase cold start even though it made the embedding more flexible so was ruled out.

title: Buffer over-read in TextDecoder()
body:
TextDecoder decodes a full Buffer when presented with a subarray of a Buffer:

```
$ llrt -e 'let utf8decoder = new TextDecoder(); console.log(utf8decoder.decode(Buffer.from("abcdefg", "utf8").subarray(0,1)));'
abcdefg
$ llrt -e 'let utf8decoder = new TextDecoder(); console.log(Buffer.from("abcdefg", "utf8").subarray(0,1).toString("utf8"));'
a
```

Previously, in PR #328, we have implemented the addition of settings to rustfmt.toml by @yollotltam.

- unstable_features = true

- group_imports = "StdExternalCrate"

title: Incorrect management of `set-cookie` in `Headers` class
author: nabetti1720

comments.author: richarddavison
nabetti1720
comments.body:
Thank you for your prompt confirmation.
For normal headers (other than `set-cookie`), we believe the current implementation is appropriate.
In other words, it is to connect them with comma delimiters.

As for `set-cookie`, basically, commas are not allowed in the value.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie#cookie-namecookie-value
>A `cookie-value` can optionally be wrapped in double quotes and include any US-ASCII character excluding control characters (ASCII characters 0 up to 31 and ASCII character 127), [Whitespace](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Whitespace), double quotes, commas, semicolons, and backslashes.

However, the `Expires=<date>` option is inconsistent because it is formatted to include a comma.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie#expiresdate
>Indicates the maximum lifetime of the cookie as an HTTP-date timestamp. See [Date](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Date) for the required formatting.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Date#syntax
>`Date: <day-name>, <day> <month> <year> <hour>:<minute>:<second> GMT`

These are the reasons why we thought that commas could not be used in managing multiple `set-cookie`.
Also, such a value cannot be retrieved successfully with the `get` method, so the `getSetCookie` method may exist.

Additionally, there is a way to manage it with Vec<(String,String)> but I don't think it's a good idea since it would not be lexicographical sorting and would require key searching in everything.

Another method would be to internally manage the data with `" | "` ("|" sandwiched between white spaces), etc., and return the data with the appropriate type(`Vector<String>`, String separated comma, etc.) when the method is called.

comments.author: nabetti1720
richarddavison
comments.body: I see, thanks for reporting. I think the enum approach would be best option forward. @nabetti1720 care to take a shot a this? :)

I did a little research on how this behavior is achieved in [hyper-rustls](https://github.com/rustls/hyper-rustls/).
